subtitle.english: Don't you see that your plans are discovered?

latin: Mārcus Tullius Cicerō, patrōnus clārissimus ōrātorque vehementissimus, in Senātū Rōmānō Catilīnae conjūrātiōnem<sup>1</sup> malefactaque dēnūntiat:
«Quousque tandem abūtere<sup>2</sup>, Catilīna, patientiā nostrā?
Quamdiū etiam furor iste tuus nōs ēlūdet? Quem ad fīnem sēsē effrēnāta<sup>3</sup> iactābit<sup>4</sup> audācia?

Nihilne tē nocturnum praesidium Palātī<sup>5</sup>, nihil urbis uigiliae, nihil timor populī, nihil concursus bonōrum omnium, nihil hic mūnītissimus habendī senātūs locus, nihil hōrum ōra uoltūsque mōuērunt?
Patēre<sup>6</sup> tua cōnsilia nōn sentīs? Cōnstrictam iam hōrum omnium scientiā<sup>7</sup> tenērī coniūrātiōnem tuam nōn uidēs?
Quid proxima, quid superiōre nocte ēgerīs, ubi fuerīs, quōs conuocāuerīs, quid cōnsilī cēperīs, quem nostrum<sup>8</sup> ignōrāre arbitrāris?
Ō tempora! ō mōrēs! Senātus haec intellegit, cōnsul uidet; hīc tamen uīuit.
Vīuit? Immō uērō etiam in senātum uēnit, fit pūblicī cōnsilī particeps<sup>9</sup>, notat et dēsignat oculīs ad caedem ūnumquemque nostrum.
Nōs autem, fortēs<sup>10</sup> uirī, satis facere reī pūblicae uidēmur, sī istīus furōrem ac tēla<sup>11</sup> uītāmus.
Ad mortem tē, Catilīna, dūcī iussū<sup>12</sup> cōnsulis iam prīdem oportēbat*, in tē cōnferrī* pestem quam tū in nōs omnīs<sup>13</sup> iam diū māchināris<sup>14</sup>.»
latinAccented: Mārcus Túllius Cícerō, patrṓnus clāríssimus ōrātórque vehementíssimus, in Senā́tū Rōmā́nō Catilī́nae conjūrātiṓnem<sup>1</sup> malefactáque dēnū́ntiat:
«Quoúsque tandem abū́tere<sup>2</sup>, Catilī́na, patiéntiā nostrā?
Quámdiū étiam furor iste tuus nōs ēlū́det? Quem ad fīnem sēsē effrēnā́ta<sup>3</sup> iactā́bit<sup>4</sup> audā́cia?

Nihílne tē noctúrnum praesídium Palā́tī<sup>5</sup>, nihil urbis uigíliae, nihil timor pópulī, nihil concúrsus bonṓrum ómnium, nihil hic mūnītíssimus habéndī senā́tūs locus, nihil hōrum ōra uoltū́sque mōuḗrunt?
Patḗre<sup>6</sup> tua cōnsília nōn sentīs? Cōnstríctam iam hōrum ómnium sciéntiā<sup>7</sup> tenḗrī coniūrātiṓnem tuam nōn úidēs?
Quid próxima, quid superiṓre nocte ḗgerīs, ubi fúerīs, quōs conuocā́uerīs, quid cṓnsilī cḗperīs, quem nostrum<sup>8</sup> ignōrā́re arbitrā́ris?
Ō témpora! ō mōrēs! Senā́tus haec intéllegit, cōnsul úidet; hīc tamen uī́uit.
Vī́uit? Immō uḗrō étiam in senā́tum uḗnit, fit pū́blicī cṓnsilī párticeps<sup>9</sup>, notat et dēsígnat óculīs ad caedem ūnumquémque nostrum.
Nōs autem, fortēs<sup>10</sup> úirī, satis fácere reī pū́blicae uidḗmur, sī istī́us furṓrem ac tēla<sup>11</sup> uītā́mus.
Ad mortem tē, Catilī́na, dūcī iússū<sup>12</sup> cṓnsulis iam prīdem oportḗbat*, in tē cōnférrī* pestem quam tū in nōs omnīs<sup>13</sup> iam diū māchinā́ris<sup>14</sup>.»
english: Marcus Tullius Cicero, very famous lawyer and orator full of fire, denounces before the Roman Senate the conspiracy and the misdeeds of Catiline:
«How long, then, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?
How much longer will this rage [of yours] make a mockery of us? [To what limit] will your unbridled audacity carry itself?

[Has] nothing [disturbed] you: the night guard of the Palatine, (nothing) the patrols in the city, (nothing) the fear of the people, (nothing) the gathering of all good men, (nothing) this most fortified place where the Senate is held, (nothing) the faces of those here [present]?
Do you not [see] that your plans [are discovered]? Do you not see that your conspiracy is already held fast by the knowledge of all these men?
What [you did] last night and the night before, where you were, whom you called together, what decision you took — which of us do you think [does not know it]?
O times! O morals! The Senate understands these things, the consul sees them; and yet this [man] lives.
He lives? Nay rather, he even comes into the Senate, he takes part in the public council, he marks and designates with his eyes each one of us for slaughter.
And we, brave men, [think we] do enough for the Republic if we avoid the rage and the weapons of this individual.

[It is] to death, Catiline, that you ought long ago to have been led by order of the consul; [it is] on you that the calamity [should have been] turned which you have long been plotting against us all.»

footnotes: Coniuratio (conjuratio), -onis, f., conspiracy, plot. Catiline had gathered a whole band of adventurers and planned to make a revolution to his own profit!

Abutere = abuteris, 2nd person singular future indicative of abuti (ab + uti, to use). The forms in ris (2nd pers. sg. of passive or deponent verbs) are sometimes replaced by forms in re; likewise erunt (3rd person plural of the active perfect) can be replaced by ere. E.g.: fuerunt or fuere. Here abutere (or abuteris) is a future (long e). In the present the e is short (abuteris or abutere, you abuse).

Iactare, to agitate, to toss, «frequentative» of jacio, -is, -ere, jeci, jactum, to throw (not to be confused with jaceo, -es, -ere, -ui, v.i., to be lying); jactare se, to boast; sese: reinforced form of se.
Palatium, -ii, n. (here Palati = Palatii, gen. sg.), or Palatinus Mons, the Palatine Hill, quarter of Rome.
Patere, which we met in L. 82, P. 2, is used here in the figurative sense.
Scientia: here, the fact of knowing (scire).
Nostrum (sometimes nostri), gen. of nos (gram. § 12), and not of noster. — N.B.: the first four verbs of P. 6 are perfect subjunctives.
Particeps, -ipis, adj., who takes part in (partem capere).

Do you remember (L. 83, Carmen) telum, -i, n., offensive weapon, missile (e.g.: sagitta, arrow; pilum, javelin; glans, gen. glandis, bullet; etc.)? arma, -orum, n. pl., designates rather defensive weapons (e.g.: clipeus or scutum, shield; lorica, cuirass, etc.) or weapons in general (ensis, sword; gladius, blade, etc.).
Duci, passive infinitive of ducere; not to be confused with the dative of dux, ducis, the guide. Iussus, -us, m. (or jussus), the order.

Omnis = omnes. This accusative plural of the 3rd declension, in is instead of es, is found in other authors of the same period (e.g. Virgil). Many editions reproduce this form, though it is a source of confusion. We therefore point it out to you, but only in this lesson, so that it does not surprise you when you read classical editions.
Machinari, deponent verb, to set up a war machine: a modern word that dates from more than two thousand years ago!
comments: Proverb: E fructu cognoscitur arbor. — The tree is known by its fruit.

Optimismus, pessimismus, pleonasmus, communismus, etc., are masculine words of the 2nd declension: in this declension, most words designating tendencies of the mind are masculine in us and not neuter in um. We had already seen feminines in us of Greek origin (atomus, methodus, etc.). — Multare, to condemn (to a fine), cf. capite damnare (L. 85, P. 15). Not to be confused with mulgeo, -es, -ere, mulsi, mulsum or mulctum, to milk. E.g.: hircos mulgere, to milk the billy-goats, that is to say to undertake something impossible.
N.B. — This piece is the only extract that has undergone no internal cut and no retouching.
As it is known to all Latinists, we think that you must not be unaware of it, even if only to see for yourself the clear simplicity of an author whom too many people make into a bugbear.

To put you in an entirely classical atmosphere, we have, in this text and in this text only, adopted the tonic accent marked in bold and the long a's, the spelling you will find in most scholarly works (see Preface, p. X, Remark). This will let you see how easy it is to pass from one system to the other. We have also respected the Ciceronian form which, in a few words, differs from the modern form adopted in the rest of our work. Try to find the corresponding differences yourself and, at the end of this lesson, compare your results with the list below.
Once this lesson is over, we will go back to the modern spelling.

List of peculiarities of the text (only the letters in italics differ): iactabit = jac... — Palati = Palatii. — uigiliae = vig... — uoltusque = vultus... — mouerunt = mov... — iam = jam. — coniurationem = conjurationem. — uides = vides. — conuocaueris = convocav... — consili = consilii. — uidet = vid... — Viuit = Vivit (for capitals, see preface P. X). — uenit = ven... — uiri = viri. — uidemur = vid... — uitamus = vit... — iussu = jussu. — iam = jam. — omnis = omnes.

latin: Quid interest* inter optimismum et pessimismum?
Optimismus omnia in meliōrem, pessimismus in pejōrem partem accipit.
Potesne* ambārum doctrīnārum exempla dare?
Philosophī duo per sōlitūdinem quamdam sitī cōnfectī trānseunt*.
Inveniunt lagōnam litrī magnitūdine sed in quā aquā ad dīmidium tantum continētur.
Prīmus, quī optimismum colit: «Eugē! inquit! fortūna nōs juvat, ecce lagōna sēmiplēna est!».
Alter autem quī pessimismum: «Ēheu! ait, fortūna nōs dēficit: semivacua est ista lagōna!»
In viā cūstōs urbānus raedārum discursiōnem moderātur.
Rēctōrī cuidam: «Tū, inquit, prōrsus prōgredere».
Rēctor, vir satis litterātus: «Quid aurēs meae audiunt? Pleonasmum!»
Cūstōs autem quī hujus vōcis significātiōnem nōn intellēxit: «Quid? maledicta in magistrātum cōnjicis: pecūniā tē multābō!»
latinAccented: Quid intérest* inter optimísmum et pessimísmum?
Optimísmus ómnia in meliṓrem, pessimísmus in pejṓrem partem áccipit.
Potésne* ambā́rum doctrīnā́rum exémpla dare?
Philósophī duo per sōlitū́dinem quamdam sitī cōnféctī trā́nseunt*.
Invéniunt lagṓnam litrī magnitū́dine sed in quā aquā ad dīmídium tantum continḗtur.
Prīmus, quī optimísmum colit: «Éugē! inquit! fortū́na nōs juvat, ecce lagṓna sēmiplḗna est!».
Alter autem quī pessimísmum: «Ḗheu! ait, fortū́na nōs dḗficit: semivácua est ista lagṓna!»
In viā cūstōs urbā́nus raedā́rum discursiṓnem moderā́tur.
Rēctṓrī cúidam: «Tū, inquit, prōrsus prōgrédere».
Rēctor, vir satis litterā́tus: «Quid aurēs meae áudiunt? Pleonásmum!»
Cūstōs autem quī hujus vōcis significātiṓnem nōn intellḗxit: «Quid? maledícta in magistrā́tum cṓnjicis: pecū́niā tē multā́bō!»
english: What is the difference between optimism and pessimism?
Optimism takes everything [by the better] (side), pessimism by the worse (part).
Can you give examples of (these) two doctrines?
Two philosophers dying of thirst cross [a] desert.
They find a bottle of a litre [in size] (grandeur), but in which [there is only half a litre of water] (water only half is contained).
The first, who [is an optimist] (cultivates optimism): «Hurrah! he said, luck is on our side (helps us), here is a bottle half full!»
The other [the pessimist] (who cultivates pessimism): «Damn! he said, luck abandons us: this bottle is half empty!»
In the street a [policeman] (urban guard) regulates the circulation of cars.
To a driver: «You, he said, go forward ahead!».
The driver, [a fairly well-read man]: «What do my ears hear? A pleonasm!».
But the policeman, who had not understood the meaning of this word: «What? You throw insults at the authority: I'll fine you!».
